podcast.title: CMA Awards (1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, Freddie Fender achieved significant recognition in country music, winning CMA Single of the Year, Male Vocalist of the Year, and Album of the Year, primarily for his work related to "Before the Next Teardrop Falls." "It was the CMA single of the year in 75. He won male vocalist of the year in 75. He got album of the year."

podcast.title: "Born Loser Records" Identity
podcast.body: Freddie Fender expressed a preference for singing what he called "Born Loser Records," as he could identify best with their themes, reflecting his own interesting life experiences. "You know, Freddie Fender said that he liked to sing what he called the Born Loser Records because he could identify best with them."

podcast.title: Bilingual Recordings
podcast.body: Following his release from prison, Freddie Fender recorded several bilingual records in an effort to revive his career. This approach ultimately led to his breakthrough success with "Before the Next Teardrop Falls." "He then recorded several bilingual records trying to get his career back on track."

podcast.title: Example of Bad Early 1970s Radio Music
podcast.body: Freddie Fender was mentioned as an example of the "bad music on the radio" in the early 1970s, which contributed to a sense of frustration among some listeners. "People like Freddie Fender and Billy Swan and Paper Lace, but let's not."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marijuana Arrest and Prison
podcast.body: After recording "Wasted Days and Wasted Nights" in 1959, Fender was arrested for marijuana possession, resulting in a three-year prison sentence. Despite being in Angola, he was still permitted to make records, suggesting he wasn't considered a major threat. "It was starting to get some traction when he was arrested for marijuana possession and that got him three years in prison."

podcast.title: Name Change from Baldemar Huerta
podcast.body: In 1958, Baldemar Huerta changed his name to Freddie Fender at the suggestion of his manager. The manager believed an "American name" would make it easier for "gringos" to read on jukeboxes. He chose "Fender" from an amplifier and "Freddie" was a spontaneous choice, noting the 'y' made it look good on promotional materials. "Well, I changed it in 1958. I had been recording under my name of Baldemar Wertha with a Hispanic label out of Macaulan, Texas, and I had a manager."
